tool.name: SQL
tool.tagline: The standard language for querying and managing relational databases
tool.description: SQL is the declarative language used to define, query and change data in relational databases such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite. It is how backends, analysts and data tools talk to stored data, and it has outlived every trend for fifty years. This curriculum uses PostgreSQL as the reference dialect and notes where others differ.

concepts.name: Tables, rows and the relational model
concepts.summary: Relational databases store data as tables of typed columns and rows, linked by matching values rather than pointers.
concepts.why: Every SQL statement you will ever write operates on tables, so the mental model comes before the syntax.
concepts.body:
A relational database keeps data in **tables** (formally, relations). Each table describes one kind of thing and has a fixed set of named, typed **columns**; each **row** is one instance of that thing. Throughout these lessons we use one small shop:

```sql
customers(id, name, email, city)
products(id, name, category, price)
orders(id, customer_id, status, total, ordered_at)
order_items(order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price)
```

Tables do not point at each other. They share values instead: `orders.customer_id` holds the `id` of a customer, and a query matches the two up when you need both. Because relationships are just matching values, you can combine any tables on any columns at query time, including combinations nobody planned for when the schema was designed.

SQL is **declarative**. You describe the result you want ("London customers, sorted by name") and the database's planner decides how to produce it: which index to use, which table to read first. You never write the loops yourself.

A few facts to internalise early:

- Rows have no inherent order. If you need an order, you must ask for one.
- Every column has a type, and every value must fit it or be `NULL` (unknown).
- Most tables have a **primary key**: a column whose value identifies each row uniquely, like `customers.id`.

SQL is an ISO standard, but every product speaks its own dialect. These lessons use PostgreSQL as the reference and point out where MySQL, SQL Server, SQLite or Oracle behave differently.
concepts.code:
-- The customers table: 4 rows, 4 columns
SELECT * FROM customers;
--  id | name  | email             | city
--   1 | Ana   | ana@example.com   | Yerevan
--   2 | Ben   | ben@example.com   | London
--   3 | Chloe | chloe@example.com | London
--   4 | Dev   | dev@example.com   | NULL

-- orders.customer_id holds a customers.id value
SELECT id, customer_id, status, total, ordered_at FROM orders;
--  id  | customer_id | status    | total  | ordered_at
--  101 |           1 | shipped   |  68.50 | 2026-01-05
--  102 |           1 | pending   | 189.00 | 2026-02-10
--  103 |           2 | shipped   |   9.99 | 2026-02-11
--  104 |           3 | cancelled |  49.00 | 2026-03-01
--  105 |           2 | shipped   | 238.00 | 2026-03-15

-- products: 1 Keyboard 49.00, 2 Mouse 19.50, 3 Monitor 189.00 (hardware),
--           4 Ebook 9.99 (digital)
takeaways: A table is a set of rows; every row has the same typed columns
Relationships are expressed by storing matching key values, not pointers
SQL is declarative: say what you want, the planner decides how
pitfalls: Assuming rows come back in insertion order. Without ORDER BY the order is unspecified and can change between runs.

quiz.q: How does a row in orders record which customer placed it?
options: It stores a pointer to the customer row's location on disk
Orders are physically nested inside the customers table
It stores the customer's id value in its customer_id column
The database remembers it from the order rows were inserted in
quiz.explain: Relational tables link through matching values: customer_id holds the id of the related customer.

quiz.q: What does it mean that SQL is declarative?
options: You describe the result and the database chooses how to compute it
Every variable must be declared before use
Queries run top to bottom exactly as written
Tables must be declared in the same file as the query
quiz.explain: You state what you want; the planner picks indexes, join order and algorithms.

concepts.name: SELECT: reading data
concepts.summary: Read columns from a table with SELECT ... FROM, choosing exactly which columns you need.
concepts.why: SELECT is the statement you will write most; everything else in querying builds on its shape.
concepts.body:
A query starts with `SELECT`, lists the columns you want, and names the table with `FROM`:

```sql
SELECT name, city FROM customers;
```

The result is itself a table: a set of rows with the columns you asked for. `SELECT *` returns every column, which is handy when exploring in a console but a bad habit in application code. It fetches data you do not use, breaks when someone adds or reorders columns, and hides from readers which columns the code actually depends on. Name the columns.

Some syntax rules that trip people up:

- Keywords are case-insensitive. `select` and `SELECT` are the same; uppercase keywords are just a readability convention.
- String literals use **single** quotes: `'London'`. Double quotes are for identifiers such as `"Order Total"`, a column name with a space or capital letters. MySQL accepts double-quoted strings by default; PostgreSQL and the standard do not.
- Unquoted identifiers are folded to lower case in PostgreSQL, so `SELECT Name FROM Customers` works on a table created as `customers`.
- A statement ends with `;`. Consoles like `psql` need it; most client libraries do not.

PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server let you `SELECT` without a table, which is useful for quick calculations: `SELECT 2 + 3;`. Oracle requires `FROM dual`.

Although you write `SELECT` first, the database logically evaluates `FROM` first: it identifies the rows, then filters and groups them, and only then computes the select list. Keeping that order in mind explains many rules you will meet later.
concepts.code:
SELECT name, city FROM customers;
--  name  | city
--  Ana   | Yerevan
--  Ben   | London
--  Chloe | London
--  Dev   | NULL

SELECT id, name, price FROM products;
--  id | name     | price
--   1 | Keyboard |  49.00
--   2 | Mouse    |  19.50
--   3 | Monitor  | 189.00
--   4 | Ebook    |   9.99

SELECT 2 + 3 AS answer;   -- no table needed in PostgreSQL
--  answer
--       5
takeaways: SELECT columns FROM table returns a new result table
Prefer explicit column lists to SELECT * in application code
Single quotes for strings, double quotes for identifiers
pitfalls: Writing "London" with double quotes in PostgreSQL: it is read as a column name and fails with 'column does not exist'.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, what does SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = "London" do?
options: Returns no rows because the comparison is case-sensitive
Fails, because "London" is treated as a column name
quiz.explain: Double quotes delimit identifiers, so PostgreSQL looks for a column called London and errors.

quiz.q: Why is SELECT * discouraged in application code?
options: It is slower to parse than a column list
It fetches unneeded data and silently changes when the table's columns change
It cannot be combined with WHERE
It returns rows in random order
quiz.explain: Explicit columns make dependencies visible and keep results stable when the schema evolves.

concepts.name: Expressions, aliases and DISTINCT
concepts.summary: Compute new columns with expressions, rename them with AS, and remove duplicate rows with DISTINCT.
concepts.why: Real queries rarely return raw columns; they compute, rename and de-duplicate.
concepts.body:
The select list can contain any **expression**, not just column names. Arithmetic, string concatenation and function calls are all fine, and each produces a column in the result:

```sql
SELECT name, price, price * 1.2 AS price_with_vat FROM products;
```

`AS` gives the output column a name (an **alias**). Without one, PostgreSQL invents a name such as `?column?`, which is awkward to read in client code. The `AS` keyword is optional for column aliases, but writing it avoids confusion when a comma goes missing: `SELECT name city` silently returns `name` labelled as `city`.

Strings are joined with `||` in PostgreSQL, SQLite and Oracle. MySQL treats `||` as logical OR by default and uses `CONCAT()`; SQL Server uses `+` or `CONCAT()`. `CONCAT()` works almost everywhere.

Watch the types in arithmetic. Dividing two integers gives an integer in PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite: `7 / 2` is `3`. Make one side numeric (`7 / 2.0`, or `CAST(x AS numeric)`, or the PostgreSQL shorthand `x::numeric`) when you want a fraction. MySQL is the odd one out and returns `3.5000`.

`DISTINCT` removes duplicate rows from the result. It applies to the whole row, not to the first column:

```sql
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM customers;      -- Yerevan, London, NULL
SELECT DISTINCT city, name FROM customers; -- all 4 rows, each pair is unique
```

DISTINCT is a sort or hash over the whole result, so it is not free. If you find yourself adding it to hide duplicates from a join, the join is usually wrong.
concepts.code:
SELECT name,
       price,
       price * 1.2               AS price_with_vat,
       name || ' (' || category || ')' AS label
FROM products;
--  name     | price  | price_with_vat | label
--  Keyboard |  49.00 |        58.800 | Keyboard (hardware)
--  Mouse    |  19.50 |        23.400 | Mouse (hardware)
--  Monitor  | 189.00 |       226.800 | Monitor (hardware)
--  Ebook    |   9.99 |        11.988 | Ebook (digital)

SELECT 7 / 2 AS int_div, 7 / 2.0 AS num_div;
--  int_div | num_div
--        3 |  3.5000000000000000

SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products;
--  hardware
--  digital
takeaways: Any expression can appear in the select list; name it with AS
Integer / integer truncates in PostgreSQL; cast to numeric for fractions
DISTINCT de-duplicates whole rows, not a single column
pitfalls: Using DISTINCT to paper over duplicate rows caused by a missing join condition.

quiz.q: What does SELECT DISTINCT city, name FROM customers return for our four customers?
options: 4 rows, because every (city, name) pair is different
An error: DISTINCT accepts only one column
quiz.explain: DISTINCT compares whole result rows; all four (city, name) combinations are unique.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, what is SELECT 5 / 2?
quiz.explain: Both operands are integers, so the division is integer division and truncates to 2.

concepts.name: Filtering rows with WHERE
concepts.summary: Keep only the rows that satisfy a condition, combining comparisons with AND, OR and NOT.
concepts.why: Almost every real query, update and delete targets a subset of rows chosen by WHERE.
concepts.body:
`WHERE` filters rows before anything else happens to them. Only rows for which the condition is **true** make it into the result:

```sql
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped';
```

Comparison operators are `=`, `<>` (the standard "not equal"; `!=` also works in every major database), `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`. Note the single `=`: SQL has no `==`. String comparison is exact and, in PostgreSQL, case-sensitive: `'london'` does not equal `'London'`. MySQL's default collations compare case-insensitively, a common surprise when moving between the two.

Combine conditions with `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`. `AND` binds tighter than `OR`, exactly like multiplication and addition, so this query does not do what it seems to say:

```sql
-- shipped orders over 50, OR any order at all from customer 1
WHERE status = 'shipped' AND total > 50 OR customer_id = 1
```

Add parentheses whenever you mix `AND` and `OR`; it costs nothing and removes the doubt.

Because `WHERE` runs before the select list is computed, you cannot refer to a column alias defined in `SELECT`. Repeat the expression, or wrap the query in a subquery, which you will see later.

The same `WHERE` clause appears in `UPDATE` and `DELETE`, where getting it wrong changes the wrong rows. A good habit: write and run the `SELECT` version first, check the rows, then turn it into the modifying statement.
concepts.code:
SELECT id, customer_id, total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'shipped' AND total > 50;
--  id  | customer_id | total
--  101 |           1 |  68.50
--  105 |           2 | 238.00

-- Parentheses make the intent explicit
SELECT id, status
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (status = 'pending' OR total < 100);
--  id  | status
--  101 | shipped
--  102 | pending

-- Aliases from SELECT are NOT visible in WHERE:
-- SELECT total * 1.2 AS gross FROM orders WHERE gross > 100;  -- ERROR
SELECT id, total * 1.2 AS gross FROM orders WHERE total * 1.2 > 100;
takeaways: WHERE keeps rows whose condition is true
AND binds tighter than OR; parenthesise mixed logic
SELECT aliases cannot be used in WHERE
pitfalls: Forgetting parentheses around an OR, so the filter matches far more rows than intended.

quiz.q: Which rows does WHERE status = 'shipped' OR status = 'pending' AND total > 100 match?
options: Orders that are (shipped or pending) and over 100
All shipped orders, plus pending orders over 100
No rows; the expression is ambiguous and errors
quiz.explain: AND is evaluated first, so the condition reads shipped OR (pending AND total > 100).

quiz.q: Why does SELECT total * 2 AS dbl FROM orders WHERE dbl > 100 fail?
options: Arithmetic is not allowed in WHERE
AS cannot be used with numeric columns
WHERE is evaluated before the select list, so the alias does not exist yet
quiz.explain: Logically FROM and WHERE run before SELECT computes and names its output columns.

concepts.name: IN, BETWEEN and LIKE
concepts.summary: Match against lists, ranges and text patterns with IN, BETWEEN and LIKE.
concepts.why: These operators make common filters shorter and clearer than chains of OR and comparisons.
concepts.body:
Three operators cover most filters that are not a single comparison.

`IN` tests membership in a list, replacing a chain of `OR`s:

```sql
WHERE status IN ('pending', 'shipped')
```

`NOT IN` is the opposite, but treat it with care: if the list contains a `NULL`, `NOT IN` matches nothing at all. The NULL lesson explains why.

`BETWEEN a AND b` is an **inclusive** range, the same as `>= a AND <= b`. That inclusiveness bites with timestamps: `ordered_at BETWEEN '2026-02-01' AND '2026-02-28'` excludes everything after midnight at the start of the 28th. For time ranges use a half-open interval instead:

```sql
WHERE ordered_at >= '2026-02-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-03-01'
```

`LIKE` matches text patterns. `%` matches any run of characters (including none) and `_` matches exactly one character:

- `name LIKE 'M%'` starts with M
- `email LIKE '%@example.com'` ends with that domain
- `name LIKE '_o%'` has o as its second letter

In PostgreSQL `LIKE` is case-sensitive; `ILIKE` is a PostgreSQL-only case-insensitive version (elsewhere, compare `LOWER(name) LIKE 'm%'`). To match a literal `%` or `_`, escape it with a backslash: `LIKE '50\%%'`.

Performance note: a pattern with a fixed prefix (`'M%'`) can use an index in the right conditions, but a leading wildcard (`'%book'`) forces the database to examine every row. PostgreSQL's trigram indexes (the `pg_trgm` extension) exist precisely for that case.
concepts.code:
SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE status IN ('pending', 'cancelled');
--  102 | pending
--  104 | cancelled

SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 19.50 AND 49.00;
--  Keyboard | 49.00     <- both ends are included
--  Mouse    | 19.50

SELECT id FROM orders
WHERE ordered_at >= '2026-02-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-03-01';
--  102
--  103

SELECT name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'M%';
--  Mouse
--  Monitor

SELECT name FROM products WHERE name ILIKE '%BOOK';  -- PostgreSQL only
--  Ebook
takeaways: IN replaces OR chains; NOT IN breaks if the list contains NULL
BETWEEN includes both ends; use >= and < for time ranges
LIKE: % = any run of characters, _ = one character; ILIKE is PostgreSQL's case-insensitive form
pitfalls: Using BETWEEN with a date upper bound on a timestamp column and silently losing the last day's rows.

quiz.q: Which names match name LIKE '_o%'?
quiz.explain: _ matches one character and then the second letter must be o: Mouse and Monitor both qualify.

quiz.q: Why is ordered_at >= '2026-02-01' AND ordered_at < '2026-03-01' preferred over BETWEEN for February?
options: BETWEEN's inclusive upper bound misses times later on the last day or double-counts boundaries
BETWEEN does not work with dates
BETWEEN is exclusive at the upper end
quiz.explain: A half-open range covers every instant in the month exactly once, regardless of time precision.

concepts.name: NULL and three-valued logic
concepts.summary: NULL means unknown; comparisons with it are neither true nor false, so you test it with IS NULL.
concepts.why: Misunderstanding NULL is the single most common source of silently wrong SQL results.
concepts.body:
`NULL` is not zero, not an empty string, and not a value at all: it is a marker for **unknown** or missing data. Dev's `city` is NULL because we do not know it.

Any comparison with an unknown value produces an unknown result. `NULL = NULL` is not true; it is NULL. So SQL uses **three-valued logic**: conditions evaluate to true, false or unknown, and `WHERE` keeps only rows where the condition is true. That has consequences:

- `WHERE city = NULL` matches nothing. Use `WHERE city IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`.
- `WHERE city <> 'London'` does not return Dev, because `NULL <> 'London'` is unknown.
- Arithmetic with NULL yields NULL: `price + NULL` is NULL. So does `'a' || NULL` in PostgreSQL (Oracle treats the empty string as NULL, a notorious difference).

The nastiest trap is `NOT IN` with a NULL in the list. `x NOT IN (1, NULL)` means `x <> 1 AND x <> NULL`; the second part is unknown, so the whole thing can never be true and the query returns no rows. This happens most often with a subquery: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM ...)` breaks as soon as one `customer_id` is NULL. `NOT EXISTS`, covered later, does not have this problem.

When you do want "equal, treating NULLs as equal", PostgreSQL and the standard offer `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`: `a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b` is true when both are NULL. To substitute a default for NULL, use `COALESCE(city, 'unknown')`, which returns its first non-NULL argument.

Decide deliberately whether a column may be NULL. If a value is always required, declare the column `NOT NULL` and the whole class of problems disappears.
concepts.code:
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city = NULL;      -- 0 rows!
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city IS NULL;     -- Dev

SELECT name FROM customers WHERE city <> 'London';
--  Ana            <- Dev is missing: NULL <> 'London' is unknown

SELECT name FROM customers
WHERE city IS DISTINCT FROM 'London';
--  Ana
--  Dev

SELECT name, COALESCE(city, 'unknown') AS city FROM customers;
--  Ana   | Yerevan
--  Ben   | London
--  Chloe | London
--  Dev   | unknown

SELECT 1 WHERE 3 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL);              -- 0 rows!
takeaways: NULL means unknown; comparing with it yields unknown, not true or false
Test with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, never = NULL
NOT IN with any NULL in the list returns no rows
COALESCE supplies a fallback for NULL values
pitfalls: Expecting WHERE col <> 'x' to include rows where col is NULL.

quiz.q: What does SELECT NULL = NULL return?
quiz.explain: Comparing two unknowns gives unknown, which SQL represents as NULL.

quiz.q: orders.customer_id contains a NULL in one row. What does SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) return?
quiz.explain: With a NULL in the list, every NOT IN test evaluates to unknown, so no row qualifies.

concepts.name: Sorting and limiting results
concepts.summary: Sort results with ORDER BY, and return only the first rows with LIMIT / FETCH FIRST.
concepts.why: Top-N lists, paging and any result shown to a human need a defined order.
concepts.body:
Without `ORDER BY` the database returns rows in whatever order is cheapest, and that order can change when data or plans change. If order matters, ask for it:

```sql
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC;
```

`ASC` (the default) sorts ascending, `DESC` descending. List several keys to break ties: `ORDER BY city, name` sorts by city, then by name within each city. You can sort by an expression or by a select-list alias, because `ORDER BY` runs after `SELECT`.

Where NULLs go differs by database. PostgreSQL and Oracle treat NULL as larger than every value, so NULLs come last in ascending order and first in descending; MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server do the opposite. Be explicit with `NULLS FIRST` or `NULLS LAST` (supported by PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQLite).

To take only the first rows, PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite use `LIMIT n`, with `OFFSET m` to skip rows. The SQL standard spelling is `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY`, which PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server (after `OFFSET ... ROWS`) accept; older SQL Server code uses `SELECT TOP n`.

Two rules for limits:

- Always combine `LIMIT` with an `ORDER BY` that is **unique**. If two rows tie, which one you get is arbitrary, and paging can show a row twice or skip it. Add the primary key as a final tie-breaker.
- `OFFSET 100000` still reads and discards 100,000 rows. For deep paging, use **keyset pagination**: remember the last row's sort key and ask for `WHERE (price, id) < (49.00, 1) ORDER BY price DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`.
concepts.code:
SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 2;
--  Monitor  | 189.00
--  Keyboard |  49.00

-- Standard syntax, same result
SELECT name, price FROM products
ORDER BY price DESC
FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY;

-- NULL placement made explicit; id breaks ties deterministically
SELECT name, city FROM customers ORDER BY city NULLS FIRST, id;
--  Dev   | NULL
--  Ben   | London
--  Chloe | London
--  Ana   | Yerevan

-- Page 2 of orders, 2 per page, newest first
SELECT id, ordered_at FROM orders
ORDER BY ordered_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;
--  103 | 2026-02-11
--  102 | 2026-02-10
takeaways: Without ORDER BY, row order is undefined
Make the sort key unique (add the primary key) before using LIMIT
NULL placement differs across databases; say NULLS FIRST/LAST
Deep OFFSET is slow; keyset pagination scales
pitfalls: Paging with LIMIT/OFFSET over a non-unique sort key, so rows repeat or vanish between pages.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, where do NULL cities appear in ORDER BY city ASC?
quiz.explain: PostgreSQL treats NULL as larger than any value, so ascending order puts NULLs last by default.

quiz.q: Why can SELECT ... ORDER BY city LIMIT 1 return different customers on different runs?
options: ORDER BY is ignored when LIMIT is present
Ben and Chloe tie on city, and the order among ties is unspecified
quiz.explain: Rows with equal sort keys may come back in any order; add a unique tie-breaker such as id.

concepts.name: Aggregate functions
concepts.summary: Collapse many rows into one value with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX, and know how they treat NULL.
concepts.why: Counts, totals and averages are the first questions anyone asks of data.
concepts.body:
An **aggregate function** takes a set of rows and returns a single value. Without `GROUP BY`, the whole filtered table becomes one group and the query returns exactly one row:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(total), AVG(total) FROM orders WHERE status = 'shipped';
```

The core five are `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX`, and they share one rule: **aggregates ignore NULLs** (except `COUNT(*)`). That gives three different counts:

- `COUNT(*)` counts rows.
- `COUNT(city)` counts rows where `city` is not NULL.
- `COUNT(DISTINCT city)` counts different non-NULL values.

Ignoring NULLs also affects `AVG`: the average of 10, NULL and 20 is 15, not 10. If missing should count as zero, write `AVG(COALESCE(x, 0))`.

Over zero rows, `COUNT` returns 0 but `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` return NULL, which surprises code that expects `SUM` of nothing to be 0. Wrap it: `COALESCE(SUM(total), 0)`.

The standard `FILTER` clause (supported by PostgreSQL and SQLite) applies a condition to one aggregate only, so a single pass can compute several counts:

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'shipped') AS shipped,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending
FROM orders;
```

Elsewhere, write `SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'shipped' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

Finally, once you aggregate, you cannot also select plain columns: `SELECT name, COUNT(*) FROM customers` is an error, because there is one count but four names. To get one result per name or city, you need `GROUP BY`, the next lesson.
concepts.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)            AS orders,
       SUM(total)          AS revenue,
       ROUND(AVG(total), 2) AS avg_order,
       MAX(total)          AS biggest
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'shipped';
--  orders | revenue | avg_order | biggest
--       3 |  316.49 |    105.50 |  238.00

SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers, COUNT(city) AS with_city,
       COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS cities
FROM customers;
--  customers | with_city | cities
--          4 |         3 |      2

SELECT SUM(total) AS s, COALESCE(SUM(total), 0) AS safe
FROM orders WHERE status = 'refunded';
--  s    | safe
--  NULL |    0
takeaways: Aggregates return one value per group; without GROUP BY, one row total
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) skips NULLs; other aggregates ignore NULLs too
SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX of zero rows is NULL, not 0
FILTER (WHERE ...) restricts a single aggregate
pitfalls: Reporting COUNT(column) as a row count when the column contains NULLs.

quiz.q: customers has 4 rows and city is NULL for one of them. What is COUNT(city)?
quiz.explain: COUNT(column) skips NULL values, so only the three known cities are counted.

quiz.q: What does SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE false return?
options: An empty result with no rows
quiz.explain: An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row, and SUM over no rows is NULL.

concepts.name: GROUP BY and HAVING
concepts.summary: Aggregate per group with GROUP BY, and filter whole groups with HAVING.
concepts.why: Per-customer totals, per-day counts and per-category averages are all GROUP BY queries.
concepts.body:
`GROUP BY` splits the rows into groups that share the same values in the listed columns, then computes the aggregates once per group:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total) AS spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id;
```

The rule that follows: every column in the select list must either appear in `GROUP BY` or be inside an aggregate. Selecting `status` here would be ambiguous, since a customer has orders with several statuses. PostgreSQL relaxes this slightly: if you group by a table's primary key, you may select that table's other columns, because they are determined by the key. MySQL with `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY` disabled lets you select anything and returns an arbitrary value, which hides bugs.

`WHERE` and `HAVING` both filter, at different moments:

- `WHERE` filters **rows** before grouping. It cannot use aggregates.
- `HAVING` filters **groups** after aggregation, so it can: `HAVING SUM(total) > 200`.

The logical evaluation order makes this clear: `FROM` → `WHERE` → `GROUP BY` → `HAVING` → `SELECT` → `ORDER BY` → `LIMIT`. A condition on a plain column belongs in `WHERE`, where it reduces the work early; put only aggregate conditions in `HAVING`.

You can group by expressions, such as `date_trunc('month', ordered_at)` to get monthly figures. NULLs form their own group: all customers with an unknown city land in one NULL group.

A group exists only if at least one row falls into it. A per-customer report built from `orders` alone will never show Dev, who has no orders; to include zero rows you need an outer join, coming up in the Joins module.
concepts.code:
SELECT customer_id,
       COUNT(*)   AS orders,
       SUM(total) AS spent
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'cancelled'          -- row filter, before grouping
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total) > 200              -- group filter, after aggregation
ORDER BY spent DESC;
--  customer_id | orders | spent
--            1 |      2 | 257.50
--            2 |      2 | 247.99

SELECT date_trunc('month', ordered_at) AS month, COUNT(*)
FROM orders
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;
--  2026-01-01 00:00:00+00 | 1
--  2026-02-01 00:00:00+00 | 2
--  2026-03-01 00:00:00+00 | 2
takeaways: Each selected column must be grouped or aggregated
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after
Logical order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
Groups only exist for values present in the data
pitfalls: Putting non-aggregate conditions in HAVING instead of WHERE, which works but filters late and reads oddly.
Expecting groups with zero rows to appear in the result.

quiz.q: Where must the condition 'only customers who spent more than 200 in total' go?
quiz.explain: It depends on an aggregate over each group, so it can only be evaluated by HAVING after grouping.

quiz.q: Why is SELECT customer_id, status, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id rejected?
options: status is neither grouped nor aggregated, so its value per group is ambiguous
COUNT(*) cannot be used with GROUP BY
GROUP BY must list every column of the table
quiz.explain: A customer can have orders with different statuses, so the query does not say which one to show.

concepts.name: Creating and altering tables
concepts.summary: Define tables with CREATE TABLE, and change or remove them with ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE.
concepts.why: Before you can store data you need a table, and real schemas change over time.
concepts.body:
`CREATE TABLE` names a table and lists its columns, each with a type and optional constraints:

```sql
CREATE TABLE products (
    id       bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name     text          NOT NULL,
    category text          NOT NULL DEFAULT 'hardware',
    price    numeric(10,2) NOT NULL
);
```

A few pieces to recognise:

- `NOT NULL` forbids missing values. Make it your default and allow NULL only when "unknown" is a real state.
- `DEFAULT` supplies a value when an `INSERT` leaves the column out.
- `PRIMARY KEY` marks the identifying column; `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` makes the database number rows automatically. The keys lesson covers both.

Names: use lower-case `snake_case`. Unquoted names are case-insensitive in PostgreSQL, but a table created as `"OrderItems"` must be quoted with exactly that capitalisation forever after.

Schemas evolve, and `ALTER TABLE` changes a table in place: add or drop a column, rename one, change a type, add a constraint. Adding a nullable column, or one with a constant default, is a fast metadata-only change in PostgreSQL 11 and later, but changing a column's type usually rewrites the whole table while holding an exclusive lock. On a large production table that matters.

`DROP TABLE` removes a table and its data permanently. `IF EXISTS` / `IF NOT EXISTS` make scripts re-runnable.

One PostgreSQL strength: DDL is **transactional**. You can run `CREATE` and `ALTER` statements inside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` and roll them all back on failure. MySQL and Oracle commit implicitly on most DDL, so a half-applied migration stays half-applied.
takeaways: CREATE TABLE lists columns with types, NOT NULL, DEFAULT and keys
ALTER TABLE changes a live table; some changes rewrite and lock it
PostgreSQL DDL is transactional; MySQL and Oracle DDL commits implicitly
pitfalls: Creating mixed-case quoted names like "CustomerId" and then having to quote them in every query.

quiz.q: A table was created with CREATE TABLE "OrderItems" (...). Which query works in PostgreSQL?
quiz.explain: Quoted identifiers keep their case, and unquoted names are folded to lower case, so only the quoted form matches.

quiz.q: What happens to a column omitted from an INSERT when it has DEFAULT now()?
options: It copies the previous row's value
quiz.explain: DEFAULT supplies the value whenever an INSERT does not specify the column.

concepts.name: Choosing data types
concepts.summary: Pick the right type for numbers, money, text, booleans, dates and ids, and avoid the classic mistakes.
concepts.why: Types enforce correctness, determine storage size and decide how comparisons and arithmetic behave.
concepts.body:
Every column has a type, and choosing well prevents a whole category of bugs. The PostgreSQL types you will use most:

- **Integers**: `integer` (4 bytes, about ±2.1 billion) and `bigint` (8 bytes). Use `bigint` for ids of tables that may grow; running out of `integer` ids in production is a painful migration.
- **Exact decimals**: `numeric(p, s)`, e.g. `numeric(10,2)` for prices. Use it for money.
- **Floating point**: `real` and `double precision` are fast but inexact: `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3`. Fine for measurements, wrong for money.
- **Text**: `text` and `varchar(n)`. In PostgreSQL they perform identically; `varchar(n)` only adds a length check. Avoid `char(n)`, which pads with spaces.
- **Booleans**: `boolean`, with values `true`, `false` and NULL. MySQL emulates it with `TINYINT(1)`; SQL Server uses `bit`.
- **Dates and times**: `date`, `timestamp` (no time zone) and `timestamptz`. Prefer `timestamptz` for moments in time; it stores an absolute instant and converts to the session's time zone on display.
- **Identifiers**: `uuid` for globally unique ids, plus `jsonb`, arrays and more, covered later.

Convert between types with the standard `CAST(x AS type)` or PostgreSQL's `x::type`. Literals such as `'2026-03-01'` are untyped until context gives them a type, which is why comparing them to a `date` column just works.

Dialects differ more here than anywhere else. SQLite uses type affinity and will happily store text in an integer column. Oracle uses `NUMBER` and `VARCHAR2` and treats `''` as NULL. MySQL's `DATETIME` has no time zone, while its `TIMESTAMP` converts to UTC and has a year-2038 limit.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id bigint        NOT NULL,
    status      text          NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    total       numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,     -- exact: money
    is_gift     boolean       NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    ordered_at  timestamptz   NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8;    -- false
SELECT 0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric = 0.3;          -- true

SELECT CAST('42' AS integer) + 1;                  -- 43
SELECT '2026-03-01'::date + 30;                    -- 2026-03-31

SELECT pg_typeof(total), pg_typeof(ordered_at) FROM orders LIMIT 1;
--  numeric | timestamp with time zone
takeaways: Use numeric for money, never float
Default to bigint ids and timestamptz for points in time
text and varchar(n) perform the same in PostgreSQL
Cast with CAST(x AS t) or x::t
pitfalls: Storing prices in double precision and getting rounding errors in totals.
Using timestamp without time zone for events from users in different zones.

quiz.q: Which type should store an order total of 19.99?
quiz.explain: numeric stores decimal values exactly; binary floating point cannot represent 19.99 exactly.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, what is the practical difference between text and varchar(100)?
options: varchar(100) only adds a maximum-length check
quiz.explain: Both use the same storage; the length limit is just a constraint.

concepts.name: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE
concepts.summary: Add rows with INSERT, change them with UPDATE, remove them with DELETE, and see the affected rows with RETURNING.
concepts.why: Reading data is half the job; applications constantly create, change and remove rows.
concepts.body:
`INSERT` adds rows. Always list the target columns, so the statement does not depend on column order and omitted columns get their defaults:

```sql
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city)
VALUES ('Eve', 'eve@example.com', 'Paris'),
       ('Finn', 'finn@example.com', NULL);
```

One statement with several `VALUES` rows is much faster than many single-row inserts. `INSERT INTO t (...) SELECT ...` copies the result of a query.

`UPDATE` changes columns of the rows that match `WHERE`. The right-hand side can use the old values:

```sql
UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.10 WHERE category = 'hardware';
```

`DELETE` removes matching rows:

```sql
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';
```

The rule that saves careers: **an UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE touches every row**. Run the equivalent `SELECT` first, and when working by hand, do it inside a transaction (`BEGIN; ... ` check the row count `... COMMIT;` or `ROLLBACK;`).

`RETURNING` (PostgreSQL, SQLite and MariaDB; SQL Server's equivalent is `OUTPUT`) hands back the affected rows, so you can fetch a generated id or the new values without a second query. MySQL has no `RETURNING`; use `LAST_INSERT_ID()` there.

To empty a whole table, `TRUNCATE orders` is much faster than `DELETE FROM orders` because it does not visit rows one by one. It needs a stronger lock and does not fire row-level triggers, and in PostgreSQL it is still transactional.

Every statement reports how many rows it affected (`UPDATE 3` in psql). Check that number in application code; an update that matched zero rows is often a bug.
concepts.code:
INSERT INTO customers (name, email, city)
VALUES ('Eve', 'eve@example.com', 'Paris')
RETURNING id, name;
--  id | name
--   5 | Eve

UPDATE products
SET price = price * 1.10
WHERE category = 'hardware'
RETURNING name, price;
--  Keyboard |  53.90
--  Mouse    |  21.45
--  Monitor  | 207.90

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';   -- DELETE 1
-- looks right? COMMIT; otherwise:
ROLLBACK;
takeaways: Always list the columns in INSERT
UPDATE/DELETE without WHERE affects every row
RETURNING gives you generated ids and new values in the same round trip
TRUNCATE empties a table far faster than DELETE
pitfalls: Running an UPDATE whose WHERE clause was accidentally not selected in the SQL editor.

quiz.q: What does UPDATE products SET price = 0; do?
options: Sets the price of every product to 0
Does nothing until COMMIT in every database
quiz.explain: With no WHERE clause, every row matches the update.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of INSERT ... RETURNING id?
options: It rolls back automatically on error
It returns the generated id without a second query
quiz.explain: RETURNING sends back values from the inserted rows, including database-generated ones.

concepts.name: Primary keys and identity columns
concepts.summary: Identify every row with a primary key, usually a database-generated identity column or UUID.
concepts.why: Keys are what updates, deletes, foreign keys and joins use to find exactly one row.
concepts.body:
A **primary key** is a column, or set of columns, whose value uniquely identifies a row. Declaring one gives you three things at once: values must be unique, they may not be NULL, and the database builds a unique index to enforce that, which also makes lookups by key fast. A table has at most one primary key.

There are two schools of key:

- A **natural key** is a real-world attribute, like an ISBN or a country code. Tempting, but real-world values change and are reused more often than anyone expects.
- A **surrogate key** is a meaningless id generated by the database. It never needs to change, which is why most schemas use one, plus a `UNIQUE` constraint on the natural attribute (such as `email`).

For generated integer ids, the standard syntax, supported by PostgreSQL 10+, Oracle 12c+ and DB2, is an **identity column**. `GENERATED ALWAYS` rejects manually supplied values; `GENERATED BY DEFAULT` allows them. Older PostgreSQL code uses `serial`, which does the same job less cleanly. MySQL uses `AUTO_INCREMENT`; SQL Server uses `IDENTITY(1,1)`. Identity values come from a sequence and can have gaps after rollbacks or failed inserts: never rely on them being contiguous.

`uuid` keys can be generated anywhere (even in the client) without coordination and do not leak row counts, at the cost of 16 bytes and, for random version-4 UUIDs, scattered index inserts. Time-ordered version-7 UUIDs avoid most of that cost.

A key can span several columns. A line in `order_items` is identified by the order and the product together, so its key is `PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)`.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id    bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    name  text NOT NULL,
    email text NOT NULL UNIQUE          -- natural attribute stays unique
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id   bigint  NOT NULL,
    product_id bigint  NOT NULL,
    quantity   integer NOT NULL,
    unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)  -- composite key
);

INSERT INTO customers (name, email) VALUES ('Ana', 'ana@example.com')
RETURNING id;                           -- 1

INSERT INTO customers (id, name, email) VALUES (99, 'X', 'x@example.com');
-- ERROR: cannot insert a non-DEFAULT value into column "id"
--        (column is GENERATED ALWAYS)
takeaways: A primary key is unique, NOT NULL and automatically indexed
Prefer surrogate keys plus UNIQUE constraints on natural attributes
Use GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY (standard) rather than serial
Generated ids can have gaps; never depend on them being sequential
pitfalls: Using a changeable natural value, such as an email address, as the primary key referenced by other tables.

quiz.q: Which guarantee does a PRIMARY KEY give that a plain UNIQUE constraint does not?
quiz.explain: Both are unique and indexed, but a primary key also forbids NULL; UNIQUE allows NULLs.

quiz.q: After a failed insert, the next identity value skips a number. Why?
options: Sequences hand out values outside the transaction and do not reuse them after rollback
The primary key index was rebuilt
quiz.explain: Sequence increments are not rolled back, so gaps are normal and expected.

concepts.name: Foreign keys and referential integrity
concepts.summary: Use foreign keys so the database guarantees that every reference points at a row that exists.
concepts.why: Without them, orphaned rows creep in and every join quietly loses or invents data.
concepts.body:
A **foreign key** declares that a column's values must exist in another table's key. With

```sql
customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id)
```

the database rejects an order for a customer that does not exist, and rejects deleting a customer who still has orders. That is **referential integrity**, enforced on every write, by every application, forever. Application-level checks cannot match it, because concurrent requests and ad-hoc scripts slip past them.

What happens when the referenced row is deleted or its key changes is configurable with `ON DELETE` / `ON UPDATE`:

- `NO ACTION` / `RESTRICT` (the default behaviour): refuse the delete while references exist.
- `CASCADE`: delete the referencing rows too. Right for owned children, such as `order_items` of an order; dangerous for anything with independent value.
- `SET NULL` / `SET DEFAULT`: keep the child row and clear the reference.

The referenced columns must have a primary key or unique constraint. The referencing column, however, is **not** indexed automatically in PostgreSQL (MySQL's InnoDB does create one). Without an index, deleting a customer forces a scan of `orders` to check for references, and joins from customers to their orders are slow. Index foreign-key columns as a rule.

Foreign keys are also documentation: anyone reading the schema, and many tools, can see how tables connect. When you load data in bulk with references in a tricky order, PostgreSQL lets a constraint be `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED`, checked at commit instead of per statement.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id),
    status      text   NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    total       numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    ordered_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id);    -- not created automatically

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id   bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES orders (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    product_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES products (id),
    quantity   integer NOT NULL,
    unit_price numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (999, 10);
-- ERROR: insert or update on table "orders" violates foreign key
--        constraint "orders_customer_id_fkey"

DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 104;   -- its order_items go too (CASCADE)
DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1;  -- ERROR: still referenced from orders
takeaways: A foreign key guarantees every reference points at an existing row
ON DELETE CASCADE for owned children, RESTRICT/NO ACTION otherwise
PostgreSQL does not index the referencing column; add the index yourself
pitfalls: Relying on application code instead of foreign keys, then finding orphaned rows months later.
Putting ON DELETE CASCADE on references to valuable data, so one delete wipes out history.

quiz.q: order_items.order_id references orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. What does deleting order 101 do?
options: Deletes the order and sets order_items.order_id to NULL
Deletes the order and its order_items rows
quiz.explain: CASCADE propagates the delete to every referencing row.

quiz.q: Why should you usually create an index on orders.customer_id in PostgreSQL?
options: Foreign keys cannot be created without one
PostgreSQL does not create it automatically, and deletes on customers and joins need it
It makes the column NOT NULL
It is required for ON DELETE CASCADE syntax
quiz.explain: Only the referenced side is indexed by its key; the referencing side needs an explicit index.

concepts.name: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT
concepts.summary: Encode business rules in the schema with NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK and DEFAULT constraints.
concepts.why: Constraints stop bad data at the door, no matter which application or script writes it.
concepts.body:
Constraints turn assumptions into guarantees. The database checks them on every insert and update and rejects the statement if one fails.

- `NOT NULL`: the column must have a value.
- `UNIQUE`: no two rows share the value (or combination, for `UNIQUE (a, b)`). It is enforced by a unique index.
- `CHECK (expression)`: every row must satisfy the condition, such as `price >= 0` or `status IN ('pending', 'shipped', 'cancelled')`. A check may compare several columns of the same row, but cannot look at other rows or tables.
- `DEFAULT`: not a restriction, but declared alongside: the value used when an insert omits the column.

Two NULL subtleties matter. First, `UNIQUE` treats NULLs as distinct, so many rows may have a NULL email. PostgreSQL 15 added `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT` for the other behaviour; SQL Server, unusually, allows only one NULL. Second, a `CHECK` passes when its expression is NULL. `CHECK (price > 0)` accepts a NULL price; add `NOT NULL` if the value is required.

Name your constraints (`CONSTRAINT price_positive CHECK (...)`). The name appears in error messages, which makes failures readable, and you need it to drop the constraint later.

Adding a constraint to a big existing table must validate every row while holding a lock. PostgreSQL lets you split that: `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID` enforces the rule for new writes immediately, and a later `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` checks old rows with a much weaker lock.

Dialect note: MySQL parsed but silently ignored `CHECK` constraints until 8.0.16. Do not assume an old MySQL schema enforces what it declares.
concepts.code:
CREATE TABLE products (
    id       bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    sku      text NOT NULL,
    name     text NOT NULL,
    category text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'hardware',
    price    numeric(10,2) NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT products_sku_key  UNIQUE (sku),
    CONSTRAINT price_non_negative CHECK (price >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT category_known
        CHECK (category IN ('hardware', 'digital'))
);

INSERT INTO products (sku, name, price) VALUES ('KB-1', 'Keyboard', -5);
-- ERROR: new row for relation "products" violates check constraint
--        "price_non_negative"

-- Add a rule to a large table without a long lock
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT total_non_negative
    CHECK (total >= 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT total_non_negative;
takeaways: Constraints are enforced for every writer, unlike application checks
UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs; CHECK passes when the expression is NULL
Name constraints so errors are readable
NOT VALID + VALIDATE adds a constraint to a big table safely
pitfalls: Writing CHECK (price > 0) and assuming it also forbids a NULL price.

quiz.q: A table has email text UNIQUE (nullable). Can two rows have a NULL email in PostgreSQL by default?
options: Yes, NULLs are treated as distinct from each other
No, UNIQUE forbids duplicates including NULL
Only if the table has no primary key
quiz.explain: By default NULLs never equal each other, so they do not violate UNIQUE; NULLS NOT DISTINCT changes this.

quiz.q: Which rule can a CHECK constraint express?
options: The customer referenced by an order must exist
No two products may share a name
An order's discount must not exceed its total
A customer may have at most five orders
quiz.explain: CHECK compares columns within one row; the others need other rows or tables (foreign key, UNIQUE, triggers).

concepts.name: Inner joins
concepts.summary: Combine rows from several tables by matching key values with JOIN ... ON.
concepts.why: Normalised data lives in many tables; joins are how you put it back together for every real question.
concepts.body:
A **join** pairs rows from two tables according to a condition. The most common form, the **inner join**, keeps only pairs where the condition is true:

```sql
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.total
FROM orders AS o
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
```

`JOIN` means `INNER JOIN`. The short aliases `o` and `c` save typing and become necessary as soon as two tables share column names such as `id` or `name`. Qualify every column in a join query; it keeps the query readable and stops it breaking when someone adds a same-named column to the other table.

Think of a join as: for each order, find the customer rows that satisfy `ON`. Because a customer has many orders, the customer's columns repeat once per order. Joins **multiply** rows: a row matching three rows on the other side appears three times. That is exactly right for orders and customers, and the cause of most "my totals are too big" bugs when you join two independent one-to-many tables (say, order items and payments) to the same order and then `SUM`.

Chaining joins walks the schema. To list what each customer bought: `customers` to `orders` to `order_items` to `products`.

When the join columns have the same name on both sides, `USING (order_id)` is a shorter `ON`. A table can also be joined to itself (a **self join**) with two different aliases, for example to pair customers from the same city. `CROSS JOIN` returns every combination of rows with no condition; useful for generating grids, alarming when it happens by accident.

Older code writes joins as `FROM a, b WHERE a.id = b.a_id`. It is equivalent, but the explicit `JOIN ... ON` keeps join conditions apart from filters and makes a forgotten condition obvious.
concepts.code:
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id, p.name AS product, oi.quantity
FROM customers   AS c
JOIN orders      AS o  ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id   = o.id
JOIN products    AS p  ON p.id          = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'shipped'
ORDER BY o.id, p.name;
--  name | order_id | product  | quantity
--  Ana  |      101 | Keyboard |        1
--  Ana  |      101 | Mouse    |        1
--  Ben  |      103 | Ebook    |        1
--  Ben  |      105 | Keyboard |        1
--  Ben  |      105 | Monitor  |        1

-- Self join: pairs of customers in the same city
SELECT a.name, b.name
FROM customers a
JOIN customers b ON b.city = a.city AND a.id < b.id;
--  Ben | Chloe
takeaways: JOIN ... ON keeps pairs of rows where the condition is true
Alias tables and qualify every column
Joins multiply rows: one-to-many repeats the 'one' side
Prefer explicit JOIN syntax over comma joins
pitfalls: Joining two unrelated one-to-many tables to the same parent and summing, which inflates totals.

quiz.q: Ana has 2 orders, Ben 2, Chloe 1, Dev 0. How many rows does customers JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id return?
quiz.explain: An inner join returns one row per matching pair: 5 orders, each matched to one customer; Dev has no match.

quiz.q: Why is a.id < b.id included in the self join of customers by city?
options: To make the join use an index
Because self joins require an inequality
To drop pairs of a customer with themselves and avoid each pair appearing twice
quiz.explain: Without it, every customer pairs with itself and (Ben, Chloe) also appears as (Chloe, Ben).

concepts.name: Outer joins: LEFT, RIGHT and FULL
concepts.summary: Keep rows without a match using LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins, and find unmatched rows.
concepts.why: Reports must include customers with no orders and products never sold; inner joins silently drop them.
concepts.body:
An inner join drops rows that have no partner. Dev has no orders, so he disappears from any customers-orders inner join. An **outer join** keeps them:

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

`LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table. Where there is no match, the right table's columns are filled with NULL. `RIGHT JOIN` is the mirror image (rarely used; swap the tables and write a LEFT JOIN instead), and `FULL JOIN` keeps unmatched rows from both sides. MySQL has no `FULL JOIN`.

Those NULLs make outer joins useful for finding what is missing, a pattern called an **anti-join**:

```sql
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;          -- Dev
```

Two classic mistakes:

- **Filtering the right table in WHERE.** `LEFT JOIN orders o ... WHERE o.status = 'shipped'` removes the NULL-extended rows (NULL is not 'shipped'), quietly turning the query back into an inner join. A condition about the optional side belongs in `ON`: `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'shipped'`.
- **Counting with COUNT(*).** For Dev, the left join produces one row with NULL order columns, so `COUNT(*)` says 1. Count a column from the right table, `COUNT(o.id)`, which skips NULLs and gives 0.

When the result reads oddly, ask of each table: must a match exist (inner) or is it optional (outer)?
concepts.code:
SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(o.id)                  AS orders,   -- not COUNT(*)
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0)    AS spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
       ON o.customer_id = c.id
      AND o.status <> 'cancelled'               -- optional side: filter in ON
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY spent DESC;
--  name  | orders | spent
--  Ana   |      2 | 257.50
--  Ben   |      2 | 247.99
--  Chloe |      0 |   0
--  Dev   |      0 |   0

-- Products never ordered (anti-join)
SELECT p.name
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE oi.product_id IS NULL;
--  (no rows: every product has been ordered)
takeaways: LEFT JOIN keeps all left rows, NULL-filling missing matches
WHERE right_col IS NULL after a LEFT JOIN finds unmatched rows
Conditions on the optional table go in ON, not WHERE
Count a right-side column, not *, to get zero for no matches
pitfalls: A WHERE condition on the right table that turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join.

quiz.q: customers LEFT JOIN orders ... WHERE o.status = 'shipped'. Does Dev (no orders) appear?
options: Yes, but only if status allows NULL
No, because NULL = 'shipped' is not true, so WHERE removes his row
It depends on the join order the planner picks
quiz.explain: WHERE runs after the join and drops the NULL-extended row; move the condition into ON to keep him.

quiz.q: For a customer with no orders, what does COUNT(*) return in a customers LEFT JOIN orders GROUP BY customer query?
quiz.explain: The outer join produces one row for that customer, and COUNT(*) counts it; COUNT(o.id) would give 0.

concepts.name: Subqueries and EXISTS
concepts.summary: Nest one query inside another as a value, a list, a derived table, or an EXISTS test.
concepts.why: Many questions are easiest to express as 'rows where something about other rows is true'.
concepts.body:
A **subquery** is a `SELECT` in parentheses used inside another statement. Where it appears decides what it must return.

A **scalar subquery** returns one value and can go wherever a value can:

```sql
SELECT name, price FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);
```

A subquery after `IN` returns a single column, used as a list: `WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending')`.

A **derived table** is a subquery in `FROM`, treated like a temporary table. It is how you filter on window results or aggregate an aggregate. Most databases require an alias for it; PostgreSQL made the alias optional in version 16.

`EXISTS (subquery)` is true when the subquery returns at least one row. It usually refers to the outer row, which makes it a **correlated subquery**:

```sql
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
```

Conceptually it runs once per outer row, though the planner usually turns it into a join (a **semi-join**). What you select inside does not matter; `SELECT 1` is the convention.

Prefer `NOT EXISTS` to `NOT IN` for "rows with no match". `NOT IN` returns nothing at all if the subquery yields a single NULL, whereas `NOT EXISTS` behaves as you expect and plans as an efficient anti-join.

Subqueries versus joins: if you need columns from the other table, join. If you only need to know whether related rows exist, `EXISTS` states the intent and never duplicates outer rows, which a join to a one-to-many table would.
concepts.code:
-- Scalar subquery
SELECT name, price FROM products
WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products);    -- avg = 66.87
--  Monitor | 189.00

-- Semi-join: customers with at least one shipped order (no duplicates)
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'shipped');
--  Ana
--  Ben

-- Anti-join: customers with no orders, NULL-safe
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
--  Dev

-- Derived table: average spend per ordering customer
SELECT ROUND(AVG(spent), 2) AS avg_spent
FROM (SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
      FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) AS per_customer;
--  184.83
takeaways: Scalar subqueries return one value; IN subqueries return one column
A subquery in FROM is a derived table
EXISTS tests for related rows without duplicating outer rows
Use NOT EXISTS, not NOT IN, for 'no matching rows'
pitfalls: A scalar subquery that can return more than one row, which fails at runtime only when the data changes.

quiz.q: Why might a join to orders return Ana twice while WHERE EXISTS (...) returns her once?
options: EXISTS removes duplicates with an implicit DISTINCT
EXISTS only checks the first order
A join produces one row per matching order; EXISTS only asks whether any match exists
quiz.explain: EXISTS is a yes/no test per outer row, while a join pairs the outer row with each match.

quiz.q: What does a correlated subquery refer to?
options: A column of the outer query's current row
quiz.explain: Correlation means the inner query uses values from the row the outer query is evaluating.

concepts.name: CASE, COALESCE and NULLIF
concepts.summary: Write conditional logic inside queries with CASE, and handle NULLs with COALESCE and NULLIF.
concepts.why: Bucketing, labelling, pivoting and safe division all need if-then logic inside SQL.
concepts.body:
`CASE` is SQL's if/else expression. It returns a value, so it can appear anywhere an expression can: in `SELECT`, `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, even inside aggregates.

The **searched** form tests conditions in order and returns the first match:

```sql
CASE
    WHEN total >= 100 THEN 'large'
    WHEN total >= 20  THEN 'medium'
    ELSE 'small'
END
```

The **simple** form compares one expression with values: `CASE status WHEN 'shipped' THEN 1 WHEN 'pending' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END`. Without `ELSE`, unmatched rows get NULL. All branches must produce compatible types.

Inside an aggregate, `CASE` lets one pass compute several conditional totals, which is the portable way to **pivot** rows into columns:

```sql
SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'shipped' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS shipped_value
```

Two shorthands handle NULL:

- `COALESCE(a, b, c)` returns the first non-NULL argument. Use it for defaults: `COALESCE(city, 'unknown')`. It is standard; `IFNULL` (MySQL, SQLite), `ISNULL` (SQL Server) and `NVL` (Oracle) are two-argument dialect versions.
- `NULLIF(a, b)` returns NULL if `a = b`, otherwise `a`. Its classic use is avoiding division by zero: `x / NULLIF(y, 0)` yields NULL instead of an error.

PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle also have `GREATEST` and `LEAST` for the largest or smallest of several values. Note that in PostgreSQL they ignore NULL arguments, while in MySQL and Oracle any NULL makes the result NULL.

`CASE` is evaluated in order and stops at the first true `WHEN`, so put the narrower conditions first.
concepts.code:
SELECT id, total,
       CASE WHEN total >= 100 THEN 'large'
            WHEN total >= 20  THEN 'medium'
            ELSE 'small'
       END AS size
FROM orders ORDER BY id;
--  101 |  68.50 | medium
--  102 | 189.00 | large
--  103 |   9.99 | small
--  104 |  49.00 | medium
--  105 | 238.00 | large

-- Pivot: one row per customer, a column per status
SELECT customer_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'shipped' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS shipped,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'pending' THEN total ELSE 0 END) AS pending
FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id;
--  1 |  68.50 | 189.00
--  2 | 247.99 |   0
--  3 |   0    |   0

SELECT 10 / NULLIF(0, 0) AS safe_div;   -- NULL, not a division error
takeaways: CASE returns the value of the first true WHEN, else ELSE (or NULL)
CASE inside SUM/COUNT pivots rows into columns
COALESCE supplies defaults; NULLIF(y, 0) prevents division by zero
pitfalls: Omitting ELSE and being surprised by NULLs in the result.

quiz.q: What does CASE WHEN total > 10 THEN 'a' WHEN total > 100 THEN 'b' END give for total = 238?
quiz.explain: WHEN clauses are tested in order and the first true one wins, so 'a' is returned.

quiz.q: What does COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'x', 'y') return?
quiz.explain: COALESCE returns its first non-NULL argument.

concepts.name: String functions
concepts.summary: Clean, search, split and assemble text with SQL's string functions and pattern matching.
concepts.why: Data arrives with stray spaces, inconsistent case and combined fields; fixing it in SQL avoids round trips.
concepts.body:
Every database ships dozens of string functions. The core set, with PostgreSQL names:

- `length(s)`, `lower(s)`, `upper(s)`.
- `trim(s)` removes surrounding spaces; `ltrim`, `rtrim` remove one side.
- `substring(s FROM 2 FOR 3)` or `substr(s, 2, 3)` extracts characters; positions start at 1, not 0.
- `position('@' IN email)` finds a substring (0 if absent).
- `replace(s, 'from', 'to')` replaces every occurrence.
- `split_part(email, '@', 2)` takes the n-th field of a delimited string.
- `concat_ws(', ', a, b, c)` joins with a separator and, unlike `||`, skips NULL arguments.
- `left(s, n)`, `right(s, n)`, `lpad(s, n, '0')`.

For anything beyond `LIKE`, PostgreSQL supports POSIX regular expressions: `email ~ '^[a-z]+@'` tests a match (`~*` is case-insensitive) and `regexp_replace(phone, '[^0-9]', '', 'g')` strips non-digits.

`string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name)` is an aggregate that concatenates values across rows; MySQL calls it `GROUP_CONCAT`, Oracle and the standard `LISTAGG`.

Dialect names vary more than behaviour: SQL Server uses `LEN` (which ignores trailing spaces) and `CHARINDEX`; MySQL's `LENGTH` counts bytes, so use `CHAR_LENGTH` for characters in UTF-8 text. PostgreSQL's `length` counts characters.

Applying a function to a column in `WHERE`, such as `WHERE lower(email) = 'ana@example.com'`, normally prevents a plain index on `email` from being used. Either store data normalised or create an index on the expression itself, as the index lessons show.
concepts.code:
SELECT email,
       split_part(email, '@', 1)         AS local_part,
       upper(left(name, 1))              AS initial,
       length(name)                      AS len,
       concat_ws(' / ', name, city)      AS label   -- NULL city skipped
FROM customers ORDER BY id;
--  ana@example.com   | ana   | A | 3 | Ana / Yerevan
--  ben@example.com   | ben   | B | 3 | Ben / London
--  chloe@example.com | chloe | C | 5 | Chloe / London
--  dev@example.com   | dev   | D | 3 | Dev

SELECT trim('  Mouse  ') AS t,
       regexp_replace('+1 (555) 010-99', '[^0-9]', '', 'g') AS digits;
--  Mouse | 155501099

SELECT city, string_agg(name, ', ' ORDER BY name) AS people
FROM customers WHERE city IS NOT NULL GROUP BY city ORDER BY city;
--  London  | Ben, Chloe
--  Yerevan | Ana
takeaways: String positions start at 1
concat_ws skips NULLs; || turns the whole result NULL
string_agg (GROUP_CONCAT, LISTAGG) concatenates across rows
Functions on a column in WHERE usually bypass a plain index
pitfalls: Using MySQL's LENGTH on UTF-8 text and getting bytes instead of characters.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, what is 'Hi ' || NULL || 'there'?
quiz.explain: The || operator propagates NULL; concat or concat_ws would skip it instead.

quiz.q: Which aggregates names from many rows into one comma-separated string in PostgreSQL?
quiz.explain: string_agg is the aggregate form; concat works on values within a single row.

concepts.name: Dates, times and intervals
concepts.summary: Do date arithmetic, truncate and extract parts of timestamps, and handle time zones correctly.
concepts.why: Nearly every report is 'per day', 'last 30 days' or 'per month', and time zone bugs are subtle.
concepts.body:
PostgreSQL's date and time support is rich and mostly standard. The building blocks:

- **Current time**: `now()` (the transaction's start time, as `timestamptz`), `current_date`, `clock_timestamp()` (wall clock, changes during a transaction).
- **Intervals**: `interval '30 days'`, `interval '2 hours'`. Add them to dates and timestamps: `now() - interval '30 days'`. Subtracting two timestamps gives an interval; subtracting two `date`s gives an integer number of days.
- **Truncation**: `date_trunc('month', ordered_at)` rounds down to the start of the month. It is the workhorse of time-bucketed reports.
- **Extraction**: `extract(year FROM ordered_at)`, `extract(dow FROM ...)` (day of week, Sunday = 0), `extract(epoch FROM ...)` (seconds since 1970).
- **Formatting**: `to_char(ordered_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD')`; parsing with `to_date` and `to_timestamp`.

Time zones deserve care. A `timestamptz` stores an absolute instant (internally UTC) and is displayed in the session's `TimeZone` setting. `AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Yerevan'` converts it to that zone's local wall time. "Per day" is therefore ambiguous: whose day? Truncate in the business's zone, `date_trunc('day', ordered_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London')`, or users near midnight will be counted on the wrong day.

`generate_series(start, stop, interval)` produces a row per step. Left-joining it to your data fills in the days with no activity, so charts show zeros instead of gaps.

Dialects differ heavily here: SQL Server uses `DATEADD`, `DATEDIFF` and `GETDATE()`; MySQL uses `DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 30 DAY)` and `DATE_FORMAT`. The concepts carry over, the spelling does not.
concepts.code:
SELECT now() - interval '30 days'                AS a_month_ago,
       date '2026-03-15' - date '2026-01-05'     AS days_between,  -- 69
       extract(dow FROM date '2026-03-15')       AS weekday;       -- 0 (Sunday)

-- Revenue per month in the shop's time zone
SELECT date_trunc('month', ordered_at AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London') AS month,
       SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
--  2026-01-01 00:00:00 |  68.50
--  2026-02-01 00:00:00 | 198.99
--  2026-03-01 00:00:00 | 238.00

-- Every day of the week, including days without orders
SELECT d::date AS day, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM generate_series(date '2026-02-09', date '2026-02-15', interval '1 day') AS d
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.ordered_at::date = d::date
GROUP BY d ORDER BY d;
--  2026-02-09 | 0
--  2026-02-10 | 1
--  2026-02-11 | 1
--  2026-02-12 | 0   ...
takeaways: Store instants as timestamptz; convert with AT TIME ZONE for local-day logic
date_trunc buckets timestamps; extract pulls out parts
Timestamp arithmetic uses intervals; date minus date gives days
generate_series + LEFT JOIN fills gaps in time series
pitfalls: Grouping by UTC day for a business whose 'day' is in another time zone.

quiz.q: What does date_trunc('month', timestamp '2026-02-11 14:30') return?
quiz.explain: date_trunc rounds down to the start of the given unit, here the first instant of February.

quiz.q: Why might per-day counts differ between a London report and a Yerevan report on the same data?
options: Each day starts at a different instant in each time zone, so orders near midnight fall on different dates
Yerevan does not use the Gregorian calendar
quiz.explain: A calendar day is a time-zone-dependent range of instants.

concepts.name: Views and materialized views
concepts.summary: Save a query under a name with CREATE VIEW, or store its result with a materialized view.
concepts.why: Views give complex joins a simple name, hide detail from consumers and let you evolve tables behind a stable interface.
concepts.body:
A **view** is a stored query with a name. You query it like a table, and the database substitutes the definition each time:

```sql
CREATE VIEW customer_spend AS
SELECT c.id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS spent
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
```

A plain view stores no data and is always current. It is not inherently faster or slower than the query it contains, because the planner merges the view's definition into your query and optimises the whole thing. Views are useful for:

- giving a well-tested join or calculation one name instead of copy-pasting it,
- restricting access: grant `SELECT` on a view exposing some columns, not on the table,
- keeping an old interface working while the underlying tables change.

Simple views over a single table (no aggregates, `DISTINCT` or joins) are **automatically updatable** in PostgreSQL: `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` on the view go to the base table. Add `WITH CHECK OPTION` to stop writes that would produce rows the view cannot see.

A **materialized view** (PostgreSQL, Oracle; SQL Server has indexed views) runs the query once and stores the result. Reads are fast, but the data is a snapshot until you run `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW`. A normal refresh locks out readers while it runs; `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` keeps the old data readable, and requires a unique index on the materialized view. Use them for expensive aggregates where minutes-old data is acceptable, like dashboards.

`CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` changes a view, but only by appending columns; to rename or remove columns, drop and recreate it.
concepts.code:
CREATE VIEW customer_spend AS
SELECT c.id, c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

SELECT name, spent FROM customer_spend WHERE spent > 100 ORDER BY spent DESC;
--  Ana | 257.50
--  Ben | 247.99

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_revenue AS
SELECT date_trunc('month', ordered_at) AS month, SUM(total) AS revenue
FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY 1;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON monthly_revenue (month);       -- needed for CONCURRENTLY
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY monthly_revenue;
takeaways: A view is a named query, expanded and optimised at query time
Simple single-table views are updatable in PostgreSQL
A materialized view stores results and must be refreshed
REFRESH ... CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index but does not block readers
pitfalls: Expecting a plain view to cache results and speed up an expensive query.

quiz.q: Does querying a plain (non-materialized) view return data as of the last refresh?
options: Only if the view has an index
No, the view's query runs against current data every time
quiz.explain: A plain view stores only its definition; each query re-evaluates it.

quiz.q: What does REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY require?
options: A primary key on the base table
A unique index on the materialized view
That no rows changed since the last refresh
quiz.explain: The concurrent refresh diffs old and new contents by a unique key.

concepts.name: Index basics
concepts.summary: Speed up lookups, joins and sorts with B-tree indexes, and understand what they cost.
concepts.why: An index is the difference between a 2 ms and a 20 second query once a table holds millions of rows.
concepts.body:
Without an index, finding `orders WHERE customer_id = 2` means reading every row: a **sequential scan**. An **index** is a separate, sorted data structure that maps column values to row locations, like the index at the back of a book. The default kind, a **B-tree**, finds a value in a few page reads even among billions of rows, and also serves range conditions (`<`, `BETWEEN`, `LIKE 'abc%'` in suitable collations) and `ORDER BY` on the indexed column.

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);
```

Primary keys and `UNIQUE` constraints create indexes automatically. Foreign-key columns do not, and they are usually the first indexes you should add.

A **multicolumn index** on `(customer_id, ordered_at)` is sorted by `customer_id`, then by `ordered_at` within each customer. It serves `WHERE customer_id = 2`, and `WHERE customer_id = 2 AND ordered_at > ...`, and `WHERE customer_id = 2 ORDER BY ordered_at DESC LIMIT 10`. It is not efficient for `WHERE ordered_at > ...` alone, because the leading column is unconstrained. Put equality columns first and range or sort columns last.

Indexes are not free. Every insert, update and delete must also update every index, and each index takes disk space and memory. Add the ones your queries need; drop the ones nothing uses.

An index cannot help when the query hides the column inside an expression: `WHERE lower(email) = ...` or `WHERE ordered_at::date = ...` cannot use a plain index on that column. Also, if a condition matches a large fraction of the table, the planner will rightly choose a sequential scan instead.

On a busy production table, use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. It takes longer, but does not block writes while it builds.
takeaways: A B-tree index serves equality, ranges and ORDER BY on its columns
PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE create indexes; foreign keys do not
Multicolumn indexes: equality columns first, range/sort columns last
Each index slows writes; wrapping a column in a function bypasses it
pitfalls: Creating an index on (a, b) and expecting it to speed up queries that filter only on b.

quiz.q: Which query can efficiently use an index on orders (customer_id, ordered_at)?
quiz.explain: The index is sorted by customer_id first, so it narrows to one customer and then scans that customer's date range.

quiz.q: Why might the planner ignore an index on status for WHERE status = 'shipped'?
options: Indexes only work on numeric columns
If most rows are shipped, reading the whole table sequentially is cheaper
quiz.explain: For low-selectivity conditions, random index lookups cost more than one sequential pass.

concepts.name: Transactions and ACID
concepts.summary: Group statements with BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK so they succeed or fail as a unit.
concepts.why: Any change spanning more than one statement, like moving stock or money, is wrong without a transaction.
takeaways: BEGIN ... COMMIT makes several statements atomic; ROLLBACK undoes them
ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability
In PostgreSQL an error aborts the whole transaction unless you use a savepoint
Keep transactions short; never hold one open while waiting on users or networks
pitfalls: Leaving connections 'idle in transaction', which holds locks and blocks vacuum.

quiz.q: In PostgreSQL, a statement fails inside BEGIN ... and you then run another UPDATE. What happens?
options: The UPDATE fails: the transaction is aborted until ROLLBACK
The earlier statements are automatically committed
quiz.explain: After an error PostgreSQL rejects every command in that transaction until it is rolled back (or rolled back to a savepoint).

quiz.q: Which ACID property guarantees committed data survives a power failure?
quiz.explain: Durability means a successful COMMIT is persisted, in PostgreSQL via the write-ahead log.

concepts.name: Common table expressions (WITH)
concepts.summary: Break a complex query into named steps with WITH, and know when PostgreSQL inlines or materialises them.
concepts.why: CTEs turn nested, unreadable subqueries into a top-to-bottom pipeline a reviewer can follow.
concepts.body:
A **common table expression** (CTE) names a subquery up front with `WITH`, so the main query can use it like a table:

```sql
WITH spend AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
    FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, s.spent
FROM spend s JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id;
```

Several CTEs can be chained, separated by commas, and each may refer to the ones before it. A query becomes a readable pipeline: compute per-customer spend, then rank it, then keep the top rows. A CTE can also be referenced more than once in the main query, which a derived table cannot.

Performance used to be the catch. Before PostgreSQL 12, every CTE was an **optimisation fence**: it was computed in full and stored, and filters from the outer query were not pushed into it. Since version 12, a side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined like a subquery. You can choose explicitly: `WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (...)` forces one evaluation (useful when the CTE is expensive and used several times), and `AS NOT MATERIALIZED` forces inlining. Other databases make their own choices; SQL Server always inlines, for instance.

PostgreSQL also allows **data-modifying CTEs**: `INSERT`, `UPDATE` or `DELETE ... RETURNING` inside `WITH`. That moves rows between tables in a single statement, atomically:

```sql
WITH moved AS (
    DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled' RETURNING *
)
INSERT INTO orders_archive SELECT * FROM moved;
```

All parts of such a statement see the same snapshot of the data, so one CTE cannot see rows another CTE in the same statement just modified; pass them through `RETURNING` instead.
concepts.code:
WITH spend AS (
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
    FROM orders
    WHERE status <> 'cancelled'
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
average AS (
    SELECT AVG(spent) AS avg_spent FROM spend
)
SELECT c.name, s.spent
FROM spend s
JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id
CROSS JOIN average a
WHERE s.spent > a.avg_spent;          -- avg of 257.50 and 247.99 = 252.745
--  name | spent
--  Ana  | 257.50

-- Force a single evaluation of an expensive CTE used twice
